reason: The support cells’ curled membrane sheets suggest they wrap around the motor fibers to insulate them.
expectation: The support cells will insulate the outgoing nerve fibers.

effect: The support cells wrapped the motor fibers, completing the insulated routes; the next goal is to connect sight to muscle commands.
reaction: The segmented wrapping and gaps made the insulation more concrete.
reason: The glass reflects light toward the eyes, so pairing them should start the sight pathway.
expectation: The eyes will detect the reflected light and produce sensory information.

effect: The eyes and reflected light formed a visual information route; it still needs a connection to muscle commands.
reaction: The change in arrow color makes the shift from light to nerve information clear.
reason: The visual sensory route leads toward a central connection, so the central nervous system is the next plausible link.
expectation: The visual route will connect to the central nervous system for processing.

effect: The visual route now reaches the brain and provides the glass’s location; the system still needs an outgoing route to the muscles.
reaction: The distinction between locating the glass and producing movement is clear.
reason: Motor nerves provide the outgoing pathway needed to connect the seeing control system to muscle commands.
expectation: The control system will connect to the motor nerves so it can send commands toward the muscles.

effect: The motor nerves now connect to the control system, but their muscle endings remain unattached.
reaction: The unattached endings make the next connection clear.
reason: The outgoing motor fibers need to connect to the muscles on the arm framework.
expectation: The motor nerve endings will connect to the arm muscles.

effect: The visual and motor pathways now connect to the arm; the new goal calls for information about its position.
reaction: The inward and outward arrows clarify the two directions of communication.
reason: The stretch receptors detect changes in muscle length, which can provide information about the arm’s position.
expectation: The receptors will detect the length change and create a sensory information route.

effect: The stretch receptors formed a position information route that carries signals toward the central nervous system.
reaction: The two muscle poses make the source of the position information clear.
reason: The guided arm includes the central nervous system, so connecting the position route should bring its sensory information back.
expectation: The sensory route will connect to the guided arm’s control system and convey information about muscle length.

effect: The position route connected the muscle sensors to the central nervous system, completing the feedback goal and the chapter.
reaction: The eyes-closed inset ties the pathway back to the opening exercise in a satisfying way.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building the position information route was most worthwhile: the changing muscle length and returning nerve signals explain how the arm can be sensed without looking at it.

leastWorthwhile.text: Connecting the seeing system to motor nerves and then to the arm felt somewhat repetitive because both were predictable links, although the unattached endings made their purpose clear.

surprise.text: The segmented wrapping and gaps around motor fibers made the role of support cells more concrete than I expected.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and goal changes supplied a plausible reason for each connection.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the chapter connected sight, motor commands and position feedback in a way that made me curious how the remaining body systems will support the arm's work.
